content: Low levels of potassium or magnesium in the blood can increase the risk of QT prolongation, a condition that affects the heart's rhythm. This risk is heightened if you are taking certain medications, such as diuretics (commonly referred to as water pills), or if you experience conditions like severe sweating, diarrhea, or vomiting. Erythromycin may interfere with the effectiveness of live bacterial vaccines, such as the typhoid vaccine. Some erythromycin products may also contain sodium, which should be considered in patients with sodium-restricted diets. Infants may be at an increased risk of developing a serious stomach condition when using this medication. Additionally, erythromycin can pass into breast milk, so caution is advised for breastfeeding mothers. Drug interactions can alter the way medications work or increase the risk of serious side effects. It is important to maintain a list of all the products you use, including prescription drugs, over-the-counter medications, and herbal supplements, and share this information with your doctor and pharmacist. Certain medications can affect how erythromycin is removed from the body, potentially altering its effectiveness. Conversely, erythromycin can slow the removal of other drugs from the body, which may impact their function. This medication may interfere with specific laboratory tests, such as urine tests, potentially leading to inaccurate results. If someone overdoses on erythromycin and exhibits severe symptoms like loss of consciousness or difficulty breathing, call emergency services (911 in the U.S.) immediately. Otherwise, contact a poison control center right away. U.S. residents can call 1-800-222-1222 for assistance. Erythromycin has been prescribed for your current condition only and should not be used for other purposes unless directed by your doctor. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is close to the time of your next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your regular dosing schedule. Do not double the dose to catch up. Different brands of erythromycin may have varying storage requirements. Refer to the product packaging or consult your pharmacist for specific instructions. Do not freeze the medication or store it in the bathroom. Avoid flushing medications down the toilet or pouring them into a drain unless instructed to do so. Properly discard this product when it is expired or no longer needed. Erythromycin is used to treat a wide range of bacterial infections and may also be used to prevent certain bacterial infections. It belongs to a class of drugs known as macrolide antibiotics. This medication is effective only against bacterial infections and will not work for viral infections, such as the common cold or flu. Take this medication by mouth, with or without food, as directed by your doctor. Shake the bottle well before each dose and measure the dose carefully using a special measuring device or spoon. The dosage and duration of treatment depend on your medical condition and response to therapy. For optimal results, take this antibiotic at evenly spaced intervals. If you are using this medication to treat an infection, continue taking it for the full prescribed duration, even if symptoms improve after a few days. Stopping the medication too early may result in a return of the infection. If you are taking this medication to prevent certain bacterial infections, follow your doctor’s instructions precisely. Common side effects of erythromycin include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain or cramping, and loss of appetite. Taking the medication with food may help reduce these symptoms. Remember that this medication has been prescribed because your doctor has determined that the benefits outweigh the risks of side effects. Rarely, erythromycin may cause a severe intestinal condition due to a bacteria called Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile). This condition may occur during treatment or weeks to months after treatment has stopped. Prolonged or repeated use of this medication may result in oral thrush or a new yeast infection. A very serious allergic reaction to this drug is rare. However, seek immediate medical attention if you experience symptoms of a severe allergic reaction, such as rash, itching/swelling (especially of the face, tongue, or throat), severe dizziness, or trouble breathing. This is not a complete list of possible side effects. In the U.S., contact your doctor for medical advice about side effects. In Canada, consult your doctor for medical advice about side effects. Before taking erythromycin, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to it, other macrolide antibiotics (such as azithromycin or clarithromycin), or any other allergies. This product may contain inactive ingredients that can cause allergic reactions or other problems. Erythromycin may cause a condition that affects the heart rhythm (QT prolongation). The risk of QT prolongation may be increased if you have certain medical conditions or are taking other drugs that can cause QT prolongation. Low levels of potassium or magnesium in the blood may also increase your risk of QT prolongation. This risk may be higher if you use certain drugs (such as diuretics or water pills) or if you have conditions such as severe sweating, diarrhea, or vomiting.
